articles.title_orig: Iran’s president tells U.N. his country ‘must be powerful so as to avoid being threatened’
articles.title_zh: Iran’s president tells U.N. his country ‘must be powerful so as to avoid being threatened’
articles.content_orig:
Seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, the Iranian president stood on a podium in New York to tell President Donald Trump that the Islamic Republic “will not bow down.”
As his country confronts its gravest existential war, and amid Trump’s threats of “annihilation” and mounting economic strain at home, Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian told world leaders attending the United Nations General Assembly that Iran will not yield on its nuclear program, missile defenses or control of the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil once flowed.
“We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways,” Pezeshkian said.
The Iranian president used the world stage to deliver Tehran’s demands and Iran’s core message to Trump, who has sought through war to defeat the Islamic Republic. Trump has boasted that the United States has “blown up” nuclear sites in Iran, and he has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz. From the same podium on Tuesday, he said he was considering whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” and drive it “into hell.”
Pezeshkian’s address was among the most anticipated speeches at this year’s United Nations gathering, and delivering it on American soil was a rare historic moment: a foreign leader holding forth in an enemy country still at war with his own.
Despite Washington’s early forecasts that the fighting would be brief, the US-Israeli war on Iran has instead dragged on, turning a military operation that began with the killing of the Islamic Republic’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, into months of regional instability and one of the defining foreign policy legacies of Trump’s presidency.
One of Pezeshkian’s key messages offered a glimpse into how the Islamic Republic seeks to set its postwar regional stance, telling Iran’s neighbors that its future security must be guaranteed or the entire region will have to “live under insecurity together.”
The message carried an implicit threat, according to one expert.
“Iran was presenting regional security as indivisible, signaling that continued pressure and conflict would impose costs across the region,” Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa program at London’s Chatham House think tank, told CNN.
But the message also signals that Iran knows it will need to find a way to coexist with the rest of the region, according to another expert, Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
“This reflects an understanding that, at the end of the day, Iran will need to find an arrangement for peaceful coexistence with its neighbors,” Azizi said.
Pezeshkian delivered his speech at the UN a day after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held at least two hours of talks in New York with Trump’s peace envoy Steve Witkoff, the first sign of diplomacy between the two nations since an ill-fated agreement was signed more than three months ago.
Following Pezeshkian’s remarks, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said those talks did not yield any major breakthrough, indicating the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) from earlier this year was no longer on the cards.
A plan in June for further negotiations between Iran and the United States never came to fruition. The conflict flared instead, leaving the region sinking deeper into uncertainty over how the war would end. At home, Pezeshkian and the Iranian officials who engaged Washington diplomatically have faced scrutiny from rival hard-line factions, which regard any agreement with Trump as tantamount to surrender.
“The foreign minister must explain on which authorization was his meeting with the representative of the aggressor enemy conducted?” Ebrahim Rezaei, a hard-line lawmaker, asked Wednesday after Araghchi met Witkoff.
Pezeshkian has also drawn criticism from hard-liners for attending the meeting in New York.
“His critics expressed concern that if … he signaled any intention to compromise to the outside world, this would be interpreted as a sign of weakness and desperation and would therefore be counterproductive for Iran, which wants to end the war on its own terms,” Azizi of the Crisis Group said.
As Pezeshkian and Araghchi delivered Iran’s demands to the world and a message of coexistence to the region, security officials back home announced a more hard-line position in Iran’s negotiating tactics.
Iran’s Supreme National Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, told state media in an interview broadcast around the same time as Pezeshkian’s speech that the Islamic Republic will adopt a new framework when negotiating with the US that will require Washington to take the first step.
“Under this new framework, the era of rhetoric and negotiations for their own sake has come to an end,” Rezaei said in the interview. “Any future talks, or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, will be contingent upon Washington’s full implementation of Iran’s requirements as a precondition.”
His remarks perhaps not only sent a message to Washington but were also aimed at assuaging hard-liners skeptical of the Iranian officials negotiating in New York.
Yet as Iran conducted diplomacy at the UN and signaled future coexistence with the region, Oman’s Maritime Security Center said a ship was targeted near the Strait of Hormuz, killing one person.
“Vessels are advised to transit with caution,” the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said.

articles.title_orig: NRSC Chair Tim Scott leaves Georgia, North Carolina off his list of top Senate targets
articles.title_zh: NRSC Chair Tim Scott leaves Georgia, North Carolina off his list of top Senate targets
articles.content_orig:
A key Republican super PAC has removed $6.5 million in ad reservations from North Carolina’s Senate race for the month of October, according to media tracker AdImpact.
That decision by the GOP-aligned Old North Action comes after Semafor reported Republicans are weighing their commitment to the race because Republican candidate Michael Whatley is trailing former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper in polls. The group still has $14.5 million in reservations on the books through election day and didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Senate Leadership Fund, the main GOP Senate super PAC, also shuffled some of its reservations, removing $900,000 in broadcast buys in the state while adding $400,000 in digital ads. The group says it’s part of a regular rebalance of ad buys to maximize viewership and is set to launch new ads in North Carolina as it spends millions a week there. SLF has roughly $23.2 million reserved in North Carolina, according to AdImpact.

articles.title_orig: Judge tosses Trump's lawsuit against Des Moines Register
articles.title_zh: Judge tosses Trump's lawsuit against Des Moines Register
articles.content_orig:
Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Iowa newspaper and pollster
By Kanishka Singh and Jack Queen
WASHINGTON, Sept 23 (Reuters) - An Iowa judge on Wednesday dismissed President Donald Trump's lawsuit filed in late 2024 against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer, saying a poll that showed the Republican leader trailing before the 2024 elections was legally protected speech.
Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said Trump's lawsuit sought to stretch the law to turn speech that enjoys the highest category of legal protection under the Constitution into fraud.
"Ratings, forecasts, and predictions that reflect a subjective weighing of objective data points are not sufficiently factual to be susceptible to proof, and predicting uncertain future events is not an exact science for which a publisher may be held to account," Beattie said.
Beattie said the lawsuit was barred by the First Amendment of the Constitution, which guarantees free speech and free press rights. He also ruled that Trump's lawsuit did not fit the state fraud statutes he sued under.
The ruling came as another judge appeared skeptical at a hearing that Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House was legal, indicating he may rule against Trump in his latest clash with the media.
Trump sued the Register, its parent company Gannett and Selzer over a poll ahead of the November 2024 election that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris beating him in Iowa. He accused the newspaper and its longtime pollster of fraudulently misleading readers.
Free speech group FIRE, which represented Selzer, welcomed the ruling.
"We're pleased that the court recognized what we've said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought," FIRE chief counsel Bob Corn-Revere said in a statement.
A spokesman for Trump's personal legal team said he would appeal the ruling. He also said the Register and Gannett knowingly ran a "phony poll" in an "unlawful attempt to interfere in the 2024 presidential election and to defraud Americans into believing" Kamala Harris was winning the race.
Trump won the election, including in Iowa.
Trump's pressure campaign against media coverage he dislikes has ramped up in his second term. He has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop news programs he dislikes, called on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavored broadcast stations of their licenses, filed several lawsuits against media outlets and banned some media outlets from the White House.
(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington and Jack Queen in New York; editing by Donna Bryson, Chris Reese and Sonali Paul)

articles.title_zh: Harrison Jr. blocking out noise amid slow start for Cardinals
articles.content_orig:
The Arizona Cardinals’ season-opening victory over the Los Angeles Chargers was quickly overshadowed in Week 2, when they fell 31-7 to the defending champion Seattle Seahawks in Week 2.
Much of the postgame conversation centered on wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., who finished without a catch as Arizona’s offense struggled to find a rhythm. Last Sunday’s performance was the latest sign of a relatively quiet start to the 2026 season for the third-year receiver and No. 4 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft.
Harrison entered the league widely regarded as one of the top receiving prospects in recent memory, but he has managed just one reception for 33 yards through two games. He has yet to establish himself as a consistent part of the Cardinals’ passing game.

The concerns about Harrison’s development are not new. Injury setbacks limited him to 12 games last season, when he finished with 604 receiving yards and four touchdowns. The former Ohio State standout is still searching for his first 1,000-yard NFL season, and his slow start this year has only amplified the criticism surrounding him.

The scrutiny surrounding Harrison has recently extended beyond his production. Clips highlighting his route running and blocking have prompted some observers to question what they perceive as a lack of effort during games.
LaFleur pushed back on the criticism, arguing that Harrison’s running style should not be interpreted as a lack of effort.
"I don’t see it that way," LaFleur said. "I think his running style is different than some other people’s, I would say that. If that’s people’s narrative on him, that’s fine. I know his teammates don’t feel that way."
Harrison’s tape has shown flashes of the precise route running and polished technique that helped establish him as largely a "can’t-miss" prospect. At other times, however, he has appeared frustrated while dealing with drops or falling short of his own standards.

Even as Harrison has struggled to find his footing, other players in Arizona’s offense have flourished. Wide receiver Michael Wilson surpassed the 1,000-yard mark in 2025 and was rewarded with a contract extension this offseason.
About halfway through last season, Hall of Fame receiver Marvin Harrison Sr. criticized the Cardinals’ offense, saying it was difficult to watch his son’s team play. Arizona has since made changes to its offensive coaching staff and scheme, but those adjustments have yet to translate into improved production for Harrison.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, Sept. 23, 2026: Treasury Selloff Deepens, Sending 10-Year Yield Above 5.1%
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, Sept. 23, 2026: Treasury Selloff Deepens, Sending 10-Year Yield Above 5.1%
articles.content_orig:
Soaring Treasury yields aren't just bad for the government and its $40 trillion debt. They also threaten to raise borrowing costs, hitting everyone from homeowners to credit card users, while providing limited help to savers and potential benefits to banks.
Government debt costs leaped higher Wednesday, the product of multiple factors including a fresh report showing higher inflation pressures, surging expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in October, and an auction for 5-year notes showing that Treasury demand was weak. Competition from hyperscaler debt issuance also is seen as an aggravating factor.
Yields responded by jumping more than they have in nearly a year and a half, dating back to April 2025 when President Donald Trump first announced so-called reciprocal tariffs against U.S. trading partners. Recent market liquidity efforts pushed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have had no impact so far, with rates surging higher despite intensified buyback efforts on longer-dated debt.
The 10-year note, a benchmark for mortgages and other longer-term borrowing, saw its yield hit, 5.125%, a level not seen since prior to the global financial crisis. Similarly, the 2-year note, which typically responds to Fed rate expectations and signals rates for home equity, auto loans and other debt, climbed more than 13 basis points past 4.9% as traders priced in a strong possibility that the central bank would follow its hike last week with another in October.
One basis point equals 0.01% and yields move opposite prices.
Such moves generally portend higher borrowing rates that hit the U.S. economy where it hurts the most — consumers, who drive nearly 70% of all economic activity and hold nearly $19 trillion in total debt.
While savers will benefit with incrementally higher rates on their bank savings accounts, it's unlikely to offset the pain they'll feel elsewhere, said Dan North, senior economist with Allianz Trade North America.
"The consumer's the most important part of the economy," North said. "They're going from little tiny yields on savings to ever slightly bigger tiny yields on savings. So I don't think that really yet helps the consumer that much. But it sure does crush housing, and it [impacts] on all those personal consumer loans, the credit cards and so forth."
Indeed, the interest rate on plain-vanilla savings accounts is around 0.37% and has been on a modest decline since the Fed enacted three quarter-point cuts late in 2025, according to FDIC data.
Mortgage rates, though, have been on an entirely different trajectory and are likely to continue rising. A typical 30-year mortgage is now at 7.26%, up more than a quarter percentage point in just the past couple weeks and nearly a full point over the past year, according to Mortgage News Daily.
Credit card interest rates have been fairly steady over the past few years, but also are unlikely to stay that way if current trends hold up.
When the Fed hikes, it feeds directly into the prime rate, which is used as a baseline for adjustable-rate credit and most recently was at 7%, after rising a quarter point off last week's Fed move.
Taken together, the factors make it more expensive for consumers to borrow and less likely that they'll seek the loans and credit that fuel a lot of the activity in the $32 trillion U.S. economy.
"You raise the fed funds rate, rates in the short term and effectively all along the curve go up," North said. "If it makes it harder for somebody to buy a car, then there's less demand for cars and there's less demand for auto workers, and the economy slows down. That's sort of basic economics, but that's how it works."
There are some positives from the higher rates.
Aside from whatever benefit savers get, banks can benefit. The industry's model is based on a variety of factors that can benefit in times of higher rates, from what they can charge borrowers to the margin they earn from what they charge to what they pay depositors, as well as the opportunity to get better return on their cash.
However, even bank stocks were mostly lower Wednesday as dramatically higher yields could slow loan demand and broader economic activity, which otherwise has been solid. The Atlanta Fed is tracking GDP growth of 5.1% for the third quarter, another element that could be factoring into higher yields.
Persistently higher yields, though, pose dangers to that growth picture.
"Smaller and medium enterprises are going to be suffering the worst because they have less ability to borrow," North said. "Less availability of credit makes it more difficult."

articles.title_orig: Mark Zuckerberg debuts $1,299 Meta VR Glasses and Muse Charm pendant amid AI agent push
articles.title_zh: Mark Zuckerberg debuts $1,299 Meta VR Glasses and Muse Charm pendant amid AI agent push
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is continuing his metaverse while simultaneously pushing forward on AI agents.
At Meta Connect, the Facebook co-founder revealed on Wednesday the Meta VR Glasses, a smaller and slimmer device compared to the company's older Quest-branded family of VR headsets, and a handheld device called the Muse Charm that works with the company's recently released Muse AI personal agent. He revealed the products while speaking on stage at the annual Connect conference for developers.
Zuckerberg shared few details about what Muse Charm can do, only to say that people will be able to speak to the gadget to interact with their Meta AI agents "without having to unlock a phone or open an app." He didn't say how much it would cost, but said that Meta needs to "finalize laying out the components" and is "planning to have this ready to ship in time for the holidays in December."
"We've packed a lot of technology with this little guy," Zuckerberg said. "So, if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."
The Meta VR Glasses are slimmer and lighter than the company's older Quest-branded VR headsets, but they are also more expensive, costing $1,299 when they go on sale in spring 2027. They represent Meta's first VR device since 2024, when the company debuted the $299 Quest 3S.
The Meta VR Glasses are powered by an external puck that houses a Qualcomm processor and battery, allowing it to function as a mini-computer that also helps reduce the glasses' overall weight and size. The glasses are able to display better visuals than the older Quest headset, and contain sensors that track users' eyes and hand movements, which reduces the need to use controllers to interact with the device.
"We have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion, high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time," Zuckerberg said.

articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton's sister Freida defends nephew after firing, restraining order
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton's sister Freida defends nephew after firing, restraining order
articles.content_orig:
Dolly Parton's sister Freida defends nephew after firing, restraining order
One of Dolly Parton's sisters is addressing the firing and restraining order against her nephew amid speculation of tension within the family.
She's Alive, LLC (SAL), the entity the late country musician designed to protect her legacy after her Aug. 25 death, filed a lawsuit Sept. 22 alleging her nephew, Bryan Seaver, threatened to smear his aunt’s legacy and made violent threats against several employees. The reported lawsuit and temporary restraining order came a day after Seaver received a termination notice from his role as his late aunt's head of security.
In a brief statement shared on Instagram Sept. 23, Parton's younger sister Freida dismissed the idea of a rift within the family and expressed support for Seaver, her nephew.
"Hi I'll say this and this only: there is no feud within our family. No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly's estate," she wrote. "We all love Bryan, just as we love each other. I love you all!!"
USA TODAY reached out to Seaver through his security company for comment.
Seaver, who oversaw the "Jolene" singer's security operations for more than 20 years, is the son of the late Larry Seaver, who previously held the position, and Dolly's younger sister Cassie Parton, 75.
In addition to working to protect his aunt, her residences and her professional properties, Seaver is the CEO of Squadron Augmented Protection Services, a Nashville-based company offering executive protection, estate security, business intelligence, K-9 services and event security, according to his LinkedIn page.
What is Bryan Seaver accused of?
In a lawsuit filed in Davidson County Chancery Court on Sept. 22, She's Alive LLC (SAL) alleges that Seaver waged a campaign of threats, harassment and intimidation on Parton's family and those entrusted to protect her brand.
Seaver is accused of threatening to ruin Dolly Parton's brand partnerships unless he was paid through podcast appearances and social media, according to the lawsuit obtained by the Nashville Tennesean, part of the USA TODAY Network.
The lawsuit also claimed Seaver made "threats of real-world violence" towards the singer's staff, partners, and legal and business advisers, allegedly often invoking his background as a military contractor during the Iraq War.
"As the entity entrusted by Ms. Parton to protect and promote her life’s work for future generations, SAL must cultivate a safe work environment for employees, advisors, and partners, free from intimidation or hostility — particularly intimidation by an armed former security contractor," the lawsuit reads. "Without relief, Defendants’ calculated campaign will continue to inflict fear, to destabilize SAL’s operations, and to cause further irreparable harm."
The lawsuit said Seaver allegedly told Danny Nozell, the country music legend's former manager who was selected by Parton to run She's Alive, "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or ... pay me."
What has Bryan Seaver said?
In a statement to TMZ shared Sept. 21, Seaver said he and his teams were "dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions" taken by Nozell and Pinnacle Bank.
"We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much," the statement reads.
Seaver announced his aunt's death in an Aug. 25 video shared on social media, saying he first followed Dolly Parton on the road when he was a kid in the early 1980s and got a taste of the doors she opened for her family "to reach the potential we didn't even know was possible." In the video, he said that Dolly Parton personally asked him to reveal her death.
"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," he said in the video. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not."
Contributing: Evan Mealins, Nashville Tennessean

articles.title_orig: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says
articles.title_zh: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says
articles.content_orig:
Eight US sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide, Navy says
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment.
The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns.
Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran.
The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment.
In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew".
He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons".
While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard.
Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time".
Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions, calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable".
"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday.
"Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added.
The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended.
In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment.
US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US.
Suicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.
A study of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military.
The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988.

articles.title_orig: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.title_zh: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. and China have extended a truce to keep tariffs lower for longer and rare earths flowing, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday local time.
He was speaking on Fox News, as Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in Washington, D.C. for a state visit through Friday.
Xi and Trump agreed to a one-year trade truce at a meeting in South Korea last October. The deal, which was set to expire in November, will now be extended to Jan. 10, Bessent said. He added that Beijing needs to fulfill more deliverables.
Ahead of this week's summit, many had expected the truce would be extended by six months or longer.
Chinese state media did not immediately note Bessent's comments on the trade truce.
Xi said in an official readout for his arrival that he is confident the visit will produce "fruitful results" for both sides. He said the two countries should be partners, not rivals, and work to build a stable relationship where competition and differences are managed. The readout did not mention tariffs, rare earths or artificial intelligence.
Footage streamed on China's state broadcaster showed U.S. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump meeting Xi and First Lady of China Peng Liyuan at the foot of the Chinese leader's jet. The video did not show the U.S. and Chinese leaders shaking hands — it focused on Xi and his wife shaking hands with two children presenting them each with bouquets.
After greeting Xi, Trump told reporters he would discuss the Iran war with the Chinese leader, among "many other subjects."
Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York ahead of Xi's arrival in the U.S. The two sides discussed setting up an alert system for AI incidents, according to Bessent.
While executives of major U.S. tech companies plan to join a summit dinner on Thursday, none of their Chinese counterparts are expected to attend.
Politburo Standing Committee Member Cai Qi and China's top diplomat Wang Yi accompanied Xi, according to state media.
—CNBC's Ashlee Trujillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Meta's Next Smart Glasses Collab Is With Blackpink's Lisa
articles.title_zh: Meta's Next Smart Glasses Collab Is With Blackpink's Lisa
articles.content_orig:
Meta's next smart glasses collab is with Blackpink's Lisa
Blackpink in your upper-facial area.
Meta introduced its own smart glasses earlier this year as a cheaper option than its Ray-Ban models and a way to partner with celebrities like Kylie Jenner on exclusive designs. The company is building on that strategy at Meta Connect 2026 by partnering with Blackpink rapper Lisa on two different styles of Meta Glasses. It's also expanding its existing offerings and bringing them to more countries.
Both of the "Meta Glasses by Lisa" models feature custom elements, and one of them is a brand new style while the other is an updated take on an existing offering. The Meta Adventurer Lisa Edition are rectangular glasses with a semi-translucent Moonlit Sky frame and Blush lenses, while the new Meta Capri Lisa Edition features a darker, cat-eye frame with grey lenses.
Regardless of which you pick, you'll get a custom frame (complete with a star on the temple tips), a custom charging case with a star design and case charms shaped like Lisa's pets. In terms of the level of customization, these little adornments sound similar to the little piece of bling and mirror bar that the Kylie Jenner version of Meta Glasses feature as well. The same Meta AI, audio and camera features offered on past Meta-branded smart glasses are also available on these special edition models. And as before, they support prescription lenses.
The company is also updating its Meta Glasses by Kylie Jenner collab with a new Ivory (off-white) version of its Starfire frames. Both variants of the Lisa shades and the Kylie Jenner options start at $399. Meta is also selling a new, even cheaper version of the Meta Adventurer frame in black with a plug-in charging case for $249, which is $50 less than the usual $299 starting price for the company's smart glasses. For anyone looking for non-special edition styles, the company is also introducing an entirely new Nova design that shares similarities with Ray-Ban's Headliner style.
Alongside the launch of these new frame options, Meta is also bringing Meta Glasses to more countries. These include Singapore, South Korea, Mexico and the United Arab Emirates today, as well as Brazil in the near future.

articles.title_orig: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
articles.title_zh: Sturm Und Drang At Warner Bros Amid Paramount Merger Has Insiders Wondering If The Brand Survives
articles.content_orig:
A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount‘s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference.
The video call, which has been routine since Paramount won the $110 billion bid for Warner Bros Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration; Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar; WBD Chief Comms Officer Robert Gibbs; and HR boss Amy Girdwood. According to sources, the four conceded they didn’t have much visibility into Paramount’s plans for a newly combined company, but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison‘s two-week timeframe he provided Monday.
The name and the leadership structure of the new company will likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that might be. We heard that Girdwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures.
“It feels like a scramble,” one source said.
To say staffers were surprised by the AG settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it.
“It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the roller coaster, you felt like things were not progressing.”
Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. Ellison’s takeover of the cinematic institution founded by Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed.
Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600 million from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told.
The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, which don’t necessarily translate into job cuts, but rather by reducing inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e., real estate portfolios, data servers).
But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that.
“We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros over the past decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped WarnerMedia into the hands of Discovery.
Myriad people inside Warner Bros are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a post-merger windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the acquisition, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year: No one WB title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office, with the highest-grossing movie stateside being Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking; with its $186M net production cost and a global box office gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe DC Studios chose the wrong comic book character to adapt.
On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros marriage comes together is Digger, the $125M political satire starring Tom Cruise, directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and produced by Legendary. It opens on October 2. While domestic debut prospects are at around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like it did on One Battle After Another, as the four-time Oscar-winning filmmaker’s Doctor Strangelove-like epic is being primed as an awards-season contender. It is a chip Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule.
The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion-dollar-grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot with Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on December 18.
At Paramount, the latter epic would fall into the arms of global marketing and distribution guru (and former WB senior ranking theatrical suit) Josh Goldstine, who led the Dune franchise across two movies to a $1.12B global gross and eight Oscars.
We’ve heard on the Paramount side that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution.
“There could be more fear on the Paramount side,” says one source in the know when it comes to marketing. How’s that? Goldstine will be back together with the team he built at Warners, meaning Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing along with Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford.
There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels-led Global Networks spinoff.
Yes, Warner Bros staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs: Former EVP Comms Katie Martin Kelly, prized by Warner Bros Motion Picture group co-heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, high-tailed it for Netflix as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue for poaching.
The merger closing will likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction, no longer bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership.
“Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.”
And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal.
What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros brand.”
Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.”
For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros theatrical releases on the calendar dated between October 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a currently combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros, the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum; assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during merger talk time, and that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground.
Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit due to ongoing talks with top-tier talent including director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business for the new Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros.
Beams one optimistic Warner exec, “The new merger gives us the all the financial resources to compete on a level with the big streamers.”

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
articles.content_orig:
Iran War Updates: Iran's president calls U.S. attacks "cowardly" as Trump threatens annihilation
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, saying Iranians are "the victims of terrorism" by the U.S. and Israel and "targets of cowardly attacks."
- A commercial vessel was struck in an attack in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, killing one crew member and necessitating the evacuation of more than 20 more sailors, according to the Omani navy.
- U.S. and Iranian officials met Tuesday while both countries were at the U.N. gathering, President Trump said, shortly after threatening in his address that he may "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
8 suicide attempts by U.S. sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln strike group during its record-long deployment, Navy letter says
There were eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since it began its record-long deployment about 10 months ago, according to a letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that was obtained Wednesday by CBS News.
CNN was first to report on the letter. A Navy official confirmed it was sent Tuesday.
The deployment of the Lincoln and its approximately 5,000 crew members came under scrutiny after family members of the sailors and members of Congress raised questions last month about the conditions aboard the carrier and concerns about the mental health of its service members.
The Lincoln and its strike group were sent to the Middle East after the Iran war broke out. It has since left the region and is returning to its home base of San Diego.
A defense official told CBS News two of the suicide attempts occurred during active fighting with Iran. The letter covers the entire length of the Lincoln strike group's deployment, which began in November of last year.
The strike group includes the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all the embarked aviation squadrons.
The letter was in response to questions from Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York about reported conditions on the ship. In a statement provided to CBS News, Gillibrand said that what President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members."
That the Trump administration "can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable," she added.
U.S. blockade has redirected 115 commercial vessels, military says
The U.S. military blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has now redirected 115 commercial vessels entering or exiting Iranian ports, according to U.S. Central Command.
The total is an increase of five ships since Monday, when the military last provided an update.
The blockade has become a renewed topic of conflict as Iran and the U.S. renewed negotiations this week at the U.N. General Assembly. Representatives from the United States, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, met with Iranian officials on Tuesday and apparently found some common ground, with President Trump saying the meetings went well.
However, on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei reiterated that no deal will be signed until the U.S. removes the blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
White House responds to Iranian president's speech at U.N.
President Trump is "courageously" fighting against the Iranian regime, the White House said Tuesday in response to a question about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's speech at the U.N. General Assembly.
"The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Anna Kelly, White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement. "The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable."
Through a translator, Pezeshkian said Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."
Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian said.
Canada imposes new sanctions on Iran officials, entities
The Canadian government announced new sanctions Wednesday against several senior Iranian officials and state-run entities "for their role in the Iranian regime's brutal repression of its population."
The sanctions target five senior Iranian security and government officials and five state-run entities, the foreign ministry said in a statement, without providing specifics.
"These individuals and entities have contributed to Iran's efforts to suppress dissent and restrict fundamental freedoms of Iran's population, including through digital surveillance, censorship, unlawful violence, arbitrary detention and intimidation," the ministry said.
A protest movement in Iran sparked in late December by grievances over high living costs rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on Jan. 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths from the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Rights groups based abroad put the toll higher and accused security forces of firing at demonstrators.
Massive protests also erupted in Iran in Sep. 2022 following the death in custody of Iranian Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested for allegedly violating strict dress rules for women.
UAE sanctions local branches of Iran's Bank Melli
The UAE central bank said Wednesday that it had imposed sanctions on the Emirati branches of Iran's Bank Melli, accusing it of violating local laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.
The bank said in a statement that "it has been decided to prohibit all branches of Bank Melli Iran operating in the UAE from conducting any financial transactions to and from Iran, including trade finance and fund transfers."
It cited "non-compliance with the regulations, laws and supervisory decisions in force in the UAE, including the requirements and obligations set out under the legislation related to combating money laundering, the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing."
The announcement comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, as well as Washington's more recent economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic.
As part of that stepped-up campaign, the U.S. announced new measures at the end of August targeting Iran's trading partners, and sanctioned the director of the Dubai branch of Bank Melli.
Last month, the United Arab Emirates announced the suspension of trade and financial exchanges with Tehran.
German foreign minister: "Iran must engage constructively" in negotiations
Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, offered a direct criticism of Iranian negotiations in a meeting with his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Iran must engage constructively in talks for a sustainable solution to end the conflict in the region & unconditionally open the Strait of Hormuz, ensuring free, safe and toll-free navigation for all," he said on social media.
Wadephul's comments came as Iran continues to take a hard line in negotiations, demanding the U.S. remove its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, end the war on all fronts, release frozen or restricted assets and agree to the Oman-Iran negotiated passage through the strait, according to Iranian

articles.title_orig: OpenAI and Anthropic bosses push UN for global terms on AI
articles.title_zh: OpenAI and Anthropic bosses push UN for global terms on AI
articles.content_orig:
US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination.
Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face.
Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity.
However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation.
Michael Kratsios, a former Scale AI executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures".
"International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added.
Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks.
Trump told the UN on Tuesday he wanted to rebrand it "super intelligence" and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector.
"We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins," he said earlier this month.
Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday.
"If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman.
He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology".
He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained.
He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes".
"We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added.
Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches.
Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole".
He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety".
"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added.
"But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale."
Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure."
All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology.
Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted to being hacked by AI agents, or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI.
Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia.
The Hugging Face hack has been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industry for the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity.

articles.title_orig: Judge set to rule on Trump administration’s rationale for White House media ban
articles.title_zh: Judge set to rule on Trump administration’s rationale for White House media ban
articles.content_orig:
The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House were in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be blocked immediately.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly did not immediately rule on the request after hearing arguments from an attorney for CNN, Politico and MS NOW and a lawyer for the Justice Department.
During the roughly 45-minute hearing, Kelly, a Trump appointee, appeared particularly focused on the “due process” — or lack thereof — that the journalists whose hard passes were revoked received.
He said due process requirements laid out by the judges in earlier cases involving press access, including the appeals court, were not followed in this case. “The government says those cases were wrongly decided,” Kelly said, but he has a “duty” to apply them in this case.
In a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing, lawyers for the media outlets said the president’s “ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court.
Ted Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told Kelly he should look past the administration’s new arguments that the ban was motivated by national security concerns and focus on what Trump has said about his decision.
“He is our lead witness here,” Boutrous said, pointing to Trump’s comments over the past several days that the outlets were too “negative.”
“He keeps proving our point,” Boutrous said.
Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” DOJ attorney Michael Velchik told the judge at the hearing.
He pointed to letters the White House press office sent to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.” The letters also were filed in court.
The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia. Also cited was a Politico article about bad “vibes” at Republicans’ midterm convention.
In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said.
The White House’s letter to Politico accused it of violating professional standards, including by using anonymous sources. But one of the cited articles had been based on a press call the White House hosted, according to an invitation reviewed by The Washington Post. The reporters on the call were told to cite an anonymous “senior administration official” in their reporting on the news, according to a recording reviewed by the Post.
Politico did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday evening.
Boutrous told the judge the letters were an attempt to manufacture rationale for the policy. Trump’s directive shows the result has been prejudged, he said.
“All of a sudden this is a national security issue” — a topic Trump didn’t mention at all when he announced and spoke about the ban on Friday, Boutrous added.
He urged the judge to let his clients get back to work. “These are urgent matters. We are at war,” the lawyer said.
Boutrous added that of the four CNN stories the White House complained about in its unsigned letter, only one was by a reporter who covers the building and has a hard pass that was renewed months after the story published.
Kelly questioned the government’s arguments. “I don’t know how a letter that they got after their pass was revoked could provide them with the kind of standards they would have to conform their conduct to,” the judge said.
He did not rule from the bench but said he’d take action “as soon” as he is able.
Ahead of the court hearing, more than four dozen media outlets and groups filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the judge to side with the banned outlets. NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, was among the groups in the brief.
The administration’s reason for the ban, the filing said, was “transparently viewpoint discriminatory.”
“The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene,” the group wrote in the filing.
Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta.
Trump said Monday on Truth Social that Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday.
The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.”
Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said.
He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.”
“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.
The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.”
The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says.
CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says.
The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” the court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.”
“When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.”
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation.

articles.title_orig: Trump greets Xi Jinping at plane as Chinese leader arrives for state visit
articles.title_zh: Trump greets Xi Jinping at plane as Chinese leader arrives for state visit
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping on Wednesday evening, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington.
Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 100ft long red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and first lady Melania Trump traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan’s hands upon their arrival in the US.
It came as Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the US and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called “Busan agreement” – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies.
Bessent, who met Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire.
The pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.
The simmering trade war is one of many thorny issues Trump and Xi must confront during the visit, including the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability during the two-day visit.
On Thursday, the White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi.
There was one discordant note in the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony, when Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed that while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men.
The moment, which was widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony released by Trump’s aides later.
The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.
Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.
The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.
Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.
Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honor Xi.
“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”
Robert Mackey contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Don Cooper, pitching coach for White Sox’s 2005 World Series championship team, dies at 70
articles.title_zh: Don Cooper, pitching coach for White Sox’s 2005 World Series championship team, dies at 70
articles.content_orig:
KANSAS CITY -- When Jose Contreras was sent from the Yankees to the White Sox at the 2004 Trade Deadline, he already knew quite a bit about new manager Ozzie Guillen.
The big right-hander, known as one of the nicest players in the game, wasn’t sure what to expect from his pitching coach, Don Cooper. Those doubts were washed away as soon as Contreras met the man known by many as simply Coop.
“On the day I met him, he gave me a hug like he knew me for a long time,” Contreras told MLB.com on Wednesday. “He spoke with me in Spanish a little bit. I said, ‘Ok, that’s good. That’s what I need.’”
Contreras woke up to the awful news Wednesday of Cooper’s passing at the age of 70, as was confirmed by his family. Upon hearing of Cooper’s death, Contreras said it felt the same as losing a family member.
What the sport lost was a true baseball original. Some describe Coop as old school, but much like Frank Sinatra, he did it his way and he did it to a great deal of success from July 22, 2002, until the end of the 2020 season. He touched so many lives and made history in ‘05, presiding over four straight complete games during the White Sox five-game American League Championship Series victory over the Angels en route to a World Series sweep of the Astros.
“He was a motivator type and a confidence type guy in terms of, anybody who knew Coop, knew he was kind of an East Coast [guy], where he originally was from, fast talking, could sell something,” said White Sox first baseman Paul Konerko. “And I don’t mean that in a bad way. He could talk somebody up into thinking they were good. That’s really where I think his strength was.”
“Coop had a way of communicating to pitchers that was pretty much Coop,” said White Sox television analyst Steve Stone, who was friends with Cooper during his extended White Sox tenure. “I’m not sure I’ve ever seen anybody quite do [things] the way he wanted to do it. He was able to get his point across.”
That same attitude held true with the media. During one session, a reporter asked Cooper how John Danks was responding coming off shoulder surgery. Cooper shook his head and said something along the lines of “Pretty darn good for just having a metal rod stuck in his shoulder.”
His language wasn’t quite as PG-13 rated as the paraphrase quote might indicate. His pitchers were his guys -- his fraternity, if you will. He could talk them up. He could criticize them. But he wasn’t going to put up with anyone from the outside going after his guys.
“The people think it’s everything about baseball, baseball, baseball,” Contreras said. “He helped me a lot off the field, and my family.”
“It was because they know how much he cared,” said White Sox general manager Chris Getz, who was a player and front office member while Cooper was with the organization. “He cared about them as individuals. He made so many pitchers better through the years. He had that Northeast very direct personality that resonated really well within the White Sox culture and clubhouse and I think fans adored him as well.”
Getz spoke about making an error during a crucial point of an eventual loss to the Cubs, only to have Cooper be the first person to come to him and tell him to forget about it and get after things the next day. Contreras still talked to Cooper about his son, Joseph, a talented young hurler who is playing for Vanderbilt University.
“All the time,” said Contreras of his talks with Cooper. “He said, ‘You know what? Let him pitch. Let him throw everything. Forget about whatever happened.’”
With those words, Contreras tried to imitate Cooper’s unique vocal style before pausing, laughing and then growing introspective once again.
“Unbelievable,” Contreras said. “Very sad.”
John Ely only worked with Cooper during Spring Training, when he was called up to fill innings. But he still has nothing but positive memories of their interaction.
“He was a character but it was effortless. It was genuine,” Ely said. “He never tried to be a character. He was that way on and off the field and any time you ever talked to him. I can’t say enough about Coop. He was such a fun person to be around and no nonsense but also could joke around quite a bit.”
“Like a lot of the coaches we had on that team, he could take it as good as he could give it,” Konerko said. “He’d take abuse and give, and just had a ball doing it. That’s what I think of the most.”

articles.title_orig: Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
articles.title_zh: Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
articles.content_orig:
Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford’s son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
-    Click here to listen to this article
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Detectives are trying to trace the supplier of the drugs that Cindy Crawford’s son, Persley Gerber, fatally overdosed on in Santa Monica rehab last weekend, according to law enforcement sources.
Gerber, 27, died at a luxury rehab center in Santa Monica on Sunday.
The Santa Monica Police Department said there is no indication of foul play at this time and that they are also investigating Gerber’s apparent overdose.
The sources told The Times the investigation is in its early stages.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s office conducted an autopsy Monday but deferred a cause and manner of death pending toxicology results for substances in Gerber’s system and that is expected to take several weeks, if not months, according to the office.
Gerber had entered the Resolution Living facility in Santa Monica just hours before his death, police said.
According to Resolution Living’s website, the house is a “Mental Health Recovery Residence.” The website describes it as part of a program that includes partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient treatment for a myriad of mental health issues, including depression, trauma and addiction, and offers dual diagnosis treatment for co-occurring disorders.
Santa Monica police received a call reporting a cardiac arrest and another call for an overdose at the center. Officers arrived at Resolutions Living, a $7.7-million, seven-bedroom mansion, at about 9:35 a.m. Sunday, a law enforcement source told The Times.
Resolutions Living did not return calls seeking comment.
It has become fairly common for police to now attempt to trace back the supplier of drugs in an overdose case.
Officials confirmed this week that Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl and other drugs, including a generic version of Xanax. Federal authorities probing her death are focusing their investigation in Los Angeles and are looking into whether the actor procured nonprescription pills from an area dealer. Drug Enforcement Administration agents and local investigators have questioned several people about the circumstances of her Aug. 16 death and have focused on her taking what was described as counterfeit pills before her demise.
The death of “Friends” star Matthew Perry sparked a sprawling drug investigation. Five people were charged with conspiracy to distribute ketamine to Perry, who died from acute effects of the drug.
Little is known about the Santa Monica police probe into Gerber’s death.
L.A. attorney Brian Claypool, who handles wrongful death litigation, said the autopsy and toxicology results “will be crucial in this tragic death to ascertain legal liability.”
Attorney Glen Jonas said depending on what police find, the rehab center could face scrutiny. Both attorneys said it is likely police will look closely at staffing, how the emergency was handled and other issues.
There have been cases in the past where drugs have been delivered into rehab centers.
The family of a Riverside woman sued a sober living center after she was found dead of a drug overdose.
In 2022, Edwin Oliva, of Montebello, was sentenced to over 33 years in federal prison for providing a lethal dose of fentanyl. During the early hours of Feb. 28, 2019, Oliva gave a woman a line of drugs to snort and did not tell her the substance was fentanyl — a powerful synthetic opioid. Believing the substance to be cocaine, the victim ingested the drug, which resulted in a fatal overdose.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.title_zh: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price tags (thanks RAMageddon!).
Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
The Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch both have better battery life and performance, but higher price tags.
While the 12-inch Surface Pro started at $799.99 last year, it’s debuting on October 13th at a starting price of $1,149.99. Likewise, the 13-inch Surface Laptop was originally priced at $899.99, but it’s up to $1,199.99 this time around. There’s no base 8GB model this time, causing some of the price increase, as both devices launch with a minimum of 16GB of RAM and can be configured up to 24GB.
Pricing aside, Microsoft is promising that the six-core Snapdragon X2 Plus chips will deliver up to 18 percent more efficient battery performance, more than 60 percent faster graphics performance, and up to 95 percent faster local AI inferencing on the built-in NPU.
That’s a lot of percentages, but what it equates to on these devices is better battery life and improved performance. On the Surface Pro 12-inch Second Edition, as Microsoft calls it, that means an extra hour of web browsing (up to 13 hours in total), and on the Surface Laptop 13-inch Second Edition it’s two extra hours of web browsing usage (up to 18 hours in total).
Microsoft is using similar displays on these models as last year, so the Surface Pro 12-inch has a 2196 x 1464 (220 PPI) LCD display that runs at up to 90Hz. The Surface Laptop 13-inch still ships with a 1920 x 1280 (178 PPI) display that only runs at 60Hz. Both displays have been upgraded from 400 nits of brightness to 500 nits, though.
Port selection remains the same, too. Both devices include two USB-C 3.2 ports, and the Surface Laptop 13-inch also has a USB-A 3.2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Both also support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity.
I’m surprised that Microsoft hasn’t upgraded at least one of these smaller Surface devices with a haptic trackpad, particularly because Windows 11 now adds subtle haptic nudges, and the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with haptic feedback. Microsoft is launching a second edition of its Surface Mouse with integrated haptics, and you can read all about that here.
Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both devices will also be sold to commercial customers, and the Surface Pro 12-inch will be available in an optional 5G configuration.
